## Motivation

When we have do perform multiple hypothesis tests on the same data, we must correct for the family wise error rate (FWER). This comes from the definition of Type I Error and *independence* among $n$ hypothesis tests. 

$$
\mathbb{P}[\text{At least one Hypothesis } H_0 \text{ incorrectly rejected} \mid H_0 \text{ is the truth}] = \\
1 - \mathbb{P}[\text{None of the Hypotheses } H_0 \text{ were incorrectly rejected} \mid H_0 \text{ is the truth}] = \\
1 - (1-\alpha)^n
$$

What this means is that the more hypothesis tests we perform, the more likely we made at least one Type I error. In the past, some corrections have been proposed to correct the FWER. The most popular is the bonferonni adjustment to the $\alpha$ value (given as $\alpha_b = \frac{\alpha}{n}$). This works best with a small number of comparisons and independent hypothesis tests. This is often the most conservative adjustment possible. Other methods have been developed for dependent hypothesis tests and those that are slightly less conservative. However, for fields like genomics where they perform 1000s upon 1000s of hypothesis tests, this type of correction is way too conservative, decreasing statistical power, i.e. $\mathbb{P}[\text{Hypothesis } H_0 \text{ was rejected} \mid H_1 \text{ is the truth}]$. 

## The False Discovery Rate

The False Discovery Rate (FDR) was introduced by Benjamini and Hochberg [I need to learn how to do citations here]. Instead of correcting for the FWER, FDR accepts a small proportion of false positives in exchange for a much less conservative adjustment. For example, if the FDR is set to 0.05 and we have 20 significant hypothesis test results, we expect 1 to be a false positive on average.

The original method for FDR (**Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure**) focused on independent or positively correlated hypothesis tests. Their procedure used an adjusted p-value, called the q-value. 


**DESCRIBE THE IDEA HERE**

Here is some R code, with the main function coming from the `stats` package.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(495)
# Simulated independent hypothesis tests:
num_tests <- 100
alpha <- 0.05
p_values <- rbeta(num_tests, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 65)
hist(p_values)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](2026-10-25-FDR_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The adjusted p-value for BH gives us the q-values. We can see how many hypothesis tests are below our $\alpha$ threshold for the Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure v.s. the Bonferroni Correction for FWER. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 
sum(p.adjust(p_values, method = "BH") <= alpha)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 72
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(p.adjust(p_values, method = "bonferroni") <= alpha)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::
:::


As we can see, Bonferroni rejects no hypothesis test based on the $\alpha$ threshold. BH on the other hand gives 72 q-values below the $\alpha$ threshold. We should expect that around 4 of these hypothesis tests are incorrectly rejected. 

## Procedure for Unknown Dependencies in Hypothesis Tests

In practice, we may not be confident what the dependencies in the hypothesis tests are. In the case where they are not independent or positively correlated, the **Benjamini-Yekutieli** procedure can be used. It is a more conservative version of the Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure. 

To demonstrate, I will draw dependent draws from a multivariate normal distribution and apply 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Simulated negative-dependent hypothesis tests


p.adjust(p_values, method = "BY")
```

Just like many flexible methods in statistics, the Benjamini-Yekutieli procedure performs worse than the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure under independent / positively correlated only hypothesis tests. This can be seen with the original `p_values` data:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(p.adjust(p_values, method = "BH") <= alpha)
```
